record.name: Wisconsin Homestead Credit
record._categoriesNote: It offsets property tax or rent, so 'housing-utilities' is the closest of the six -- but it is delivered as a refundable income-tax credit, not a housing program.
record.summary: A refundable state income-tax credit for lower-income Wisconsin renters and homeowners, to offset part of the property taxes or rent they paid. You can get it even if you owe no income tax.
record.benefit: A refund of up to $1,168 (2025), based on household income and the property tax or rent you paid on your Wisconsin home. Paid as a tax refund.

steps: File Schedule H (or the simpler Schedule H-EZ) with your Wisconsin income tax return, or on its own if you do not otherwise file.
Attach your 2025 property tax bill or an original rent certificate signed by your landlord.
If claiming as disabled and under 62, attach a disability verification statement.

requiredDocuments: Property tax bill or signed rent certificate
Record of all household income for 2025
record.seasonalNote: Claimed on the annual income tax return; a claim for 2025 must generally be filed within 4 years of the original due date.

of._sourceText: You were a legal resident of Wisconsin from January 1 through December 31, 2025
You owned or rented your home in 2025
You will not be claimed as a dependent on someone else's 2025 federal income tax return (does not apply if you were 62 or older on Dec 31, 2025)
You were between ages 18 and 61 on December 31, 2025, and had earned income / You were 62 or older on December 31, 2025, or disabled
Was your household income (see section F. Definitions, #11) for 2025 less than $24,680?
Are you currently living in a nursing home and also receiving Title XIX medical assistance? (a 'Yes' disqualifies)

For each month of the entire 2025 year, did you receive either Wisconsin Works (W2) payments of any amount or county relief of $400 or more? (a 'Yes' disqualifies; W-2/county-relief months also reduce the credit)

factsNeeded.sourceText: You owned or rented your home in 2025 -- housingStatus today has renting / own-home but not 'neither' cleanly, and does not tie to Wisconsin
ages 18 and 61 ... 62 or older -- the cut point is 62, which falls inside our 'under-60' band; AGE_BANDS cannot express it (same failure as WWWP)
or disabled -- hasDisability is RESERVED; here it is a full alternative qualifying route, not a caveat

'household income' here adds back untaxed items -- SSI, most pensions, child support, W-2/kinship-care/other cash assistance, workers' comp, etc. It is a distinct quantity from annualHouseholdIncome (taxable) and from the FPL-scaled incomeAtOrBelow input
will not be claimed as a dependent
living in a nursing home and also receiving Title XIX medical assistance
each month of the entire 2025 year ... Wisconsin Works (W2) ... or county relief

unencodable: The definition of 'household income' -- section F, Definitions #11, spanning instruction pages 10-17: it adds numerous nontaxable income sources back to Wisconsin taxable income. No engine fact captures this composite.
The credit is phased out as household income rises toward $24,680 (tables on instruction pages 25-26), so 'less than $24,680' is a hard cutoff but the amount near the top is small.
Tax-exempt housing rules, moved-to-tax-exempt-housing 12-month grace, farm/business proration, married-living-together must file one combined claim.
Only one credit per household; if married and living together, only one spouse may claim.

-> 2025 Schedule H Instructions (PDF, 26 pages): 'You may be able to claim homestead credit if' list on the cover; the Step-by-step qualifying questionnaire on page ~7; 'household income' defined in section F #11 (pp. 10-17)

fetch.tool: lib-source live fetcher + pdf.ts (extractPdf) -- coordinate-based, keeps table columns

scopeColocated.scopeLocation: The Step-2 questionnaire states 'Was your household income (see section F. Definitions, #11) for 2025 less than $24,680?' -- the figure is inseparable from a cross-reference to a definition 3-10 pages later. 'Household income' is a Schedule-H term of art that adds back untaxed income; a reader who takes it to mean wages, or taxable income, or FPL-relative income will mis-decide this rule in either direction.
On the cover list. But note the '62' cut point is unusual and easy to normalise to '65' or '60' -- see facts.ts, which already approximates Homestead's 62+ to the 60-64 band.

cost.notes: 1 PDF fetch + 1 search. extractPdf produced usable structured text; the flat text was one giant line (no newlines) so grep -o with context windows was the way to pull specific figures. Reading a 26-page booklet for one rule is the expensive shape.

surprises: 'Household income' looks like the plainest possible field name and is in fact a 7-page statutory construction. This is a scope problem hiding inside a word rather than inside a table cell -- the schema's scopeColocated field, framed around figures, does not naturally capture 'the figure is fine, the noun beside it is the trap'.
